flawed_step: Step 4: the claim that the contracted graph G/T, a bridgeless cubic graph, has a 3-edge-colouring. No theorem says bridgeless cubic graphs are 3-edge-colourable; snarks such as the Petersen graph are counterexamples. G/T may have no triangle, so induction cannot be used either.
counterexample: Take the Petersen graph P and replace one vertex v with a triangle abc, joining a, b and c to v's three distinct neighbours. Call the result G. G is simple and cubic, has a triangle, and is bridgeless: deleting a triangle edge leaves abc connected, and deleting any other edge e leaves P−e connected (P is 3-edge-connected) with the triangle still connected inside. Suppose G had a 3-edge-colouring. The triangle edges get three different colours, say ab=1, bc=2, ca=3. Then the outside edges at a, b and c must be coloured 2, 3 and 1, which are all different. Contracting the triangle back to v would give a proper 3-edge-colouring of P, but P is not 3-edge-colourable. So G has no 3-edge-colouring.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
(1) Let G be a bridgeless cubic graph with a triangle T=abc. Justified: this is the hypothesis.
(2) Contract T to one vertex t to get G/T. It is cubic, and bridgeless because any bridge of G/T would also be a bridge of G. Justified. (If G is K4, G/T has parallel edges, but it is still bridgeless and cubic as a multigraph.)
(3) Any 3-edge-colouring of G/T lifts to G. Justified: if the outside edges at a, b, c have colours 1, 2, 3, colour bc=1, ca=2, ab=3; this is proper. The converse also holds: in any colouring of G, the three outside edges of T get three different colours.
(4) G/T has a 3-edge-colouring. NOT justified. Nothing in the hypotheses guarantees it. Being bridgeless and cubic is not enough (snarks exist), and G/T may have no triangle, so induction does not apply.
(5) So G has a 3-edge-colouring. Not justified, because it depends on step 4.
Because step 3 works in both directions, G is 3-edge-colourable exactly when G/T is. The statement is therefore equivalent to saying every bridgeless cubic graph that arises from such a contraction is 3-edge-colourable, and that is false. Counterexample: the Petersen graph with one vertex replaced by a triangle is simple, cubic, bridgeless and contains a triangle. If it were 3-edge-colourable, contracting the triangle would give a 3-edge-colouring of the Petersen graph, which does not exist. The statement is false.
